meta.title: codetiller: CI/CD for work done by coding agents
meta.description: codetiller takes a task from your tracker, runs a coding agent in a sandbox that holds none of your credentials, verifies the result in a fresh container and opens a draft pull request. Self-hosted on Docker or Kubernetes.

hero.title: CI/CD for work done by coding agents.
hero.lead: codetiller takes a task from your tracker, runs a coding agent in a sandbox that holds none of your credentials, verifies the result in a fresh container and opens a draft pull request. People decide what runs and what merges.
hero.sceneTitle: One task, from issue to pull request

problem.label: The problem
problem.title: An agent on a laptop has your keys, your network and your tests.
problem.lead: That is fine for one engineer watching one agent. It does not hold for a team that hands agents real tickets. codetiller treats the agent as an untrusted worker and puts plain, deterministic code around it.

rows.without: It runs where your tokens and SSH keys are.
rows.with: The sandbox holds no credential. The model key stays in a gateway, the GitHub token with the factory.

rows.without: It can reach anything your machine can reach.
rows.with: One route out: the model API, through the gateway. Dependency installs read the package registries and nothing else.

rows.without: The tests pass, because the agent changed the tests.
rows.with: A test that passed before and no longer runs fails verification. Changed test config and CI files are named in the verdict.

rows.without: It says it is done. You find out in review.
rows.with: The full suite runs on a clean export in a fresh, offline container before anything is pushed.

rows.without: Spend is whatever the agent decided to do.
rows.with: Each run has one model and one budget, enforced in the gateway and not by the agent.

rows.without: A new prompt or skill “feels better”.
rows.with: A change to how agents work is measured on a benchmark, against the noise of rerunning the same thing.

how.label: How it works
how.title: A task moves through six stations. The agent is one of them.
how.lead: Everything around the agent is plain code: checkout, verification, the pull request. A task outlives its runs, so questions, answers and review feedback stay with it.

steps.title: A task comes in
steps.body: An issue that carries your label becomes a task; so does one you create by hand. Importing never starts work: only a human queues a run.

steps.title: Preflight sizes it up
steps.body: Before the first run, a read-only agent estimates the files and concepts the work touches and lists blocking questions. Too large or unclear stops and asks you; a big task comes with a proposed split.

steps.title: The agent works in a sandbox
steps.body: An ephemeral container on a network with no route out, a workspace that survives between runs, one model and one budget. The agent ends a run with a summary, or with questions for a human.
steps.note: State: RUNNING, then REVIEW or WAITING_FOR_HUMAN

steps.title: The factory verifies
steps.body: The commit is exported clean into a fresh, offline container and the full suite runs. Only tests that passed at the base commit count, and one that stopped running counts as a failure. Type check and lint run on the same export.
steps.note: Nothing is pushed before this passes

steps.title: A draft pull request opens
steps.body: With the factory's own token, never the agent's. The pull request carries the verdict, the changed files that decide how the work is checked and, when you enable it, the notes of a second, read-only reader.

steps.title: You review, the agent resumes
steps.body: Comment `/tiller …` on the pull request and the agent picks up its session with your text. The factory verifies again and pushes to the same pull request. Merging stays with you.

trust.label: Trust boundary
trust.title: The agent is untrusted. The boundary is measured, not assumed.
trust.lead: `tiller audit` runs probes inside the agent, install and verification containers, exactly as the factory configures them, and reports each fact. Run it on every host: container networking differs between them.

routes.note: one model, one budget; the gateway adds the key
not by name, not by IP, no outside DNS
an install runs code the agent chose: it may read, never publish
the factory pushes and opens pull requests, from outside the sandbox

points.title: No credential in the sandbox
points.body: The agent's API key is the name of its run: random, worth nothing outside the gateway.

points.title: Budget enforced outside the agent
points.body: The gateway counts spend from the model API's answers and refuses further calls once the budget is spent.

points.title: The cluster is not taken on trust
points.body: On Kubernetes, every sandbox pod first proves it cannot reach the cluster API. Only then does it run the command.

trust.more: Read how the boundary is built

verify.label: Verification
verify.title: Deleting the test does not pass the test.
verify.lead: Verification compares against the task's base commit. What an agent might do to get a green run is what it looks for.

items.title: Removed or skipped tests fail
items.body: A test that passed at base and no longer runs is a failure, named in the verdict. Only a human can accept a removal.

items.title: Changed checks are called out
items.body: Test config, CI workflows, package scripts, lint and type config are listed in the verdict and on the pull request. When the suite reads a file the change touched, it runs a second time with that file as it was.

items.title: More than the tests
items.body: The repository's type check, lint and build run offline on the same clean export. What CI would be the first to say is said before anything is pushed.

items.title: A second reader, if you want one
items.body: A read-only agent reads the diff against the task and reports what tests cannot say. Advisory, never a gate: it is an agent reading agent-written code.

evals.label: Evals
evals.title: Know whether a change to your agents helped.
evals.lead: Skills, prompts and models change how agents work. codetiller runs them on a benchmark of real tasks from a repository and compares the results paired, task by task.
points: A difference counts only when it holds across tasks and exceeds rerun noise: what the same two configs give when they do not differ.
`tiller gate` prints the verdict and its evidence as markdown, for the pull request of a skill or config change.
Every run writes a manifest: commits, config hash, model, image, prompt and skill hashes. A run can be rebuilt and compared later.

install.label: Install
install.title: One Linux machine with Docker. Or a namespace in your cluster.
install.lead: The install script does everything through Docker and puts nothing else on the host. The factory, its database and every workspace live in one working directory.
install.dockerGuide: Full guide: install on a Linux server
install.localGuide: Quickstart: one task on your machine
install.doctorTitle: Then ask the installation whether it is ready
install.doctorBody: `tiller doctor` measures what a task needs: the runtime answers, a container sees a workspace where the factory put it, credentials are set, each repository is reachable. It makes no model call.
install.note: No published images yet: the install builds them from the clone.

open.label: Open source
open.title: Free, open, and yours to run.
open.lead: codetiller is licensed under Apache-2.0. There is no hosted service, no account and no licence key: you clone it, run it on your machines and bring your own model key.

points.title: Read what you run
points.body: The factory holds your GitHub token and your model key. The gateway that guards them is one file without dependencies; the whole boundary is there to be read and audited.

points.title: Nothing leaves but model calls
points.body: No telemetry and no control plane somewhere else. Model usage is billed by your provider, on your key, capped per run.

points.title: Built in the open
points.body: Issues, the roadmap and what is not built yet are public. Agents, work sources and stacks that are missing are the places to contribute.

status.label: Status
status.title: What works today, and what does not yet.
status.lead: codetiller is young. The core path is tested end to end; the second list is what a team should know before adopting it.
works: A task from issue to draft pull request, with Claude Code
GitHub: issue intake, review comments, following the repository's CI
JS/TS, Go and Python repositories, onboarded with one command
Docker on Linux, and Kubernetes on one node
Benchmarks, paired comparison and the eval gate
Dashboard: tasks, timelines, transcripts, diffs, metrics
notYet: Sign-in and roles: access is by one API token
A GitHub App identity: a personal token today
Other agents: Codex, OpenCode, local models
Published images and a Helm chart
Runs spread over several cluster nodes
Services for tests (databases), private registries, JVM

items.a: Claude Code today. The agent sits behind an adapter and transcripts are stored in a harness-neutral form, so others can follow; Codex and local models are planned, not built.
Nowhere new. The factory runs on your machine or in your cluster. Code reaches the model API through the gateway, as it does when an engineer uses the agent, and no other host.

items.q: What does it need from GitHub?
items.a: A token that can read issues, push branches and open pull requests on the repositories you add, plus read access to checks if the factory should follow CI. `tiller doctor` says what is missing, per repository.
No. It opens draft pull requests. Queuing a run and merging are human actions.

items.q: What does a run cost in model usage?
items.a: What the model API charges, capped by the budget of the run. The gateway does the counting, and the Metrics page shows cost per delivered task.

items.q: Can it run on a shared server?
items.a: Give it a machine of its own. On Docker, the factory's container holds the Docker socket, which is root on that host; the factory is trusted, and nothing it starts gets the socket.
Apache-2.0. The source is on GitHub; you run it yourself and pay only your model provider.

cta.title: Start with one repository.
cta.body: Install, add a repository, queue the first task. `tiller doctor` tells you when the installation is ready.
